slides.title: Your devices talk directly.
slides.text: No cloud in the middle. Alice's phone and Bob's laptop connect to each other, wherever they are. The layer that does this is {iroh}.
slides.deep: iroh: QUIC connections between devices, direct when possible, through a relay otherwise. Every connection is end-to-end encrypted and authenticated with the endpoint keys.

slides.title: Every device's address is a key.
slides.text: Each device has its own key pair, and its public key is its address: its {endpoint ID}. Nobody hands out addresses, and nobody can take yours.
slides.deep: The iroh endpoint ID is an Ed25519 public key. Today the iroh key is separate from the signer and vouched for by it (D28); merging the two is proposed (D31).

slides.title: Finding each other.
slides.text: On the same Wi-Fi, devices simply see each other. Further away, a device publishes where it can be reached, under its own key, and anyone with the key can look it up.
slides.deep: Local discovery via mDNS on the same network; global discovery through signed records published under the key (pkarr / DNS). A record lists the addresses where an endpoint can be reached.

slides.title: Getting through.
slides.text: Most home routers block incoming connections. iroh punches a hole from both sides at once, and usually gets a direct line. If that fails, a {relay} passes the packets along. The relay sees only sealed traffic.
slides.deep: UDP hole punching from both sides at once. If that fails, a relay forwards encrypted QUIC packets it cannot read. Connections upgrade to direct when possible.

slides.title: Both sides know who they talk to.
slides.text: Every connection is encrypted with the two devices' keys. Then the device shows its signer's link to an identity, so the other side knows: this is Alice's phone, acting for Alice.
slides.deep: The QUIC handshake proves the endpoint key. The device then presents its signer's registration in the identity history, so the peer learns which identity it is talking to.

slides.title: One line, three languages.
slides.text: Over one connection, devices speak a small {protocol} for each kind of work.
list: Docs: find the missing sealed chunks, then swap them.
Values: stream chunks by hash, checked as they arrive.
News: tell interested peers “there's something new”.
slides.deep: Each protocol is an ALPN on the same endpoint: chunk sync for Docs, blob ranges for Values, gossip for announcements.

slides.title: Sealed chunks settle in layers.
slides.text: Every sealed change has a hash. About one in 256 hashes starts with a zero byte: that change closes a chunk holding everything since the last one. One in 65,000 starts with two zero bytes and closes a bigger chunk around the smaller ones. Like layers of {sediment}: old history ends up in a few big chunks. Every device, even a carrier that reads nothing, splits at the same places.
slides.deep: Sedimentree (from Ink & Switch's Subduction): depth = number of leading zero bytes of a change's BLAKE3 hash. Depth ≥ 1 closes a chunk; deeper chunks contain shallower ones. Equal content gives an equal minimal hash. (D33)

slides.title: Finding what's missing, cheaply.
slides.text: Two devices may hold the same data and differ by only a little. They never list everything. Inside one piece of data they compare {fingerprints}; across thousands of pieces of data they swap a few tiny {summaries}. Both cost about as much as the difference, not the whole.
slides.deep: Two levels (D34, proposed): fingerprints within one piece of data, RIBLT set reconciliation across many. Both cost roughly in proportion to the difference.

slides.title: Fingerprints, step by step.
slides.text: Alice picks a fresh random seed. For each layer and loose change she holds, she sends an 8-byte fingerprint: its hash, mixed with the seed. Bob fingerprints his own with the same seed, sends what she lacks and asks for what he lacks. One and a half round trips. Thanks to the layers, even a million changes are only a few hundred fingerprints.
slides.deep: SipHash-2-4 keyed with a fresh 128-bit seed per request, giving 8 bytes per item, computed over the item's causal identity. The responder diffs u64 fingerprints and replies with what is missing in both directions: 1.5 round trips.

slides.title: Tiny summaries that peel apart.
slides.text: Across all your data, each side mixes the hashes of everything it holds into summaries: each one an XOR of a random handful of hashes, plus a count. Bob subtracts his own summaries from Alice's. Whatever both hold cancels out. A summary left with just one hash names it outright; remove that one everywhere, and the next summary opens, like peeling an onion. Alice sends more summaries until everything has peeled.
slides.deep: Rateless Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables (arXiv 2402.02668). Each coded symbol is the XOR of a pseudo-random subset of item hashes plus a count and a checksum. Peel pure symbols iteratively. About 1.35 to 1.7 × d symbols for d differences.

slides.title: A Value streams in checked chunks.
slides.text: Bob asks for a Value by its hash. Every chunk is checked against that hash as it arrives, so nobody can slip in a wrong byte. He can ask for just a range, and from several devices at once.
slides.deep: BLAKE3 verified streaming: every received range is checked against the root hash before use. Ranges can come from several peers at once.

slides.title: News travels by gossip.
slides.text: News travels by {gossip}: each peer passes it on to a few others. When Alice changes the list, her device tells the peers interested in it: “house-list has something new.” Whoever wants it fetches the new sealed chunks.
slides.deep: Gossip topic = data ID. Announcements carry only new chunk hashes, so carriers learn no author or content.

slides.title: Who may even get the bytes?
slides.text: Read decides who can open data. Three more things a rule can allow decide who can carry it: want, keep and sync. Carriers never see the rules themselves: those are sealed for readers. Whoever asks shows their own proof.
list: want: may ask for this data and receive it, sealed.
keep: may store it for good.
sync: may pass it on to others whose rules say want.
slides.deep: want, keep and sync are operations in rules, like any other. Rules are sealed for readers; a carrier only checks the proof chain that the asker presents.

slides.title: want
slides.text: Before a device sends anything, even sealed chunks, the asker shows a proof that a rule gives them {want}. The carrier checks the signatures and nothing else. A stranger gets nothing at all, not even ciphertext to count or keep. Read includes want.
slides.deep: The asker presents a proof chain: seal → owner → rule granting want to a role → the asker's identity in that role → the asker's registered signer. Valid chain: sealed chunks are sent. No chain: nothing, not even ciphertext.

slides.title: keep
slides.text: Your backup gets want and {keep}. It holds every sealed chunk, for good, and gives them back to your new phone. It has no read, so to it they're just sealed bytes.
slides.deep: keep means the carrier stores sealed chunks durably and serves them to askers holding want. It never holds a data key.

slides.title: sync
slides.text: The street's always-on peer gets {sync}. It passes your changes between Alice and Bob when they're never online at the same time. It keeps them only as long as it has to.
slides.deep: sync means the peer may forward sealed chunks to others whose rules give them want, which bridges devices that are never online at the same time.

slides.title: All the rules on one list.
slides.text: One piece of data, one owner, three roles, each with exactly what it needs.
slides.deep: One owner, three roles: readers and writers (home), a durable carrier (backup) and a forwarding carrier (street). Each role holds exactly the operations it needs.

slides.title: Alice and Bob, never online together.
slides.text: Alice ticks milk on the train and goes offline. The street's peer picks it up, the backup keeps it, and Bob's laptop gets it in the evening. Neither carrier read a word.
slides.deep: Store-and-forward over carriers: every hop checks want, holds only sealed chunks, and is replaceable. This is the local-first “cloud peer”.

slides.title: Between devices, in short.
list: Every device's address is its key.
Devices connect directly, or through a relay that sees only sealed traffic.
Docs swap missing sealed chunks; Values stream checked chunks; gossip spreads the news.
want, keep and sync decide who may carry data. Read decides who may open it.
slides.deep: iroh for connections, sedimentree for chunking, fingerprints and RIBLT for differences, want, keep and sync for who may carry.
